steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Both Kodály and Bartók collected and transcribed Hungarian folk songs — their art music transforms folk material through modernist techniques.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Bartók's polymodality combines multiple modes simultaneously, creating harmonic complexity while maintaining folk-like melodic identity.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Irregular metre (5/8, 7/8) reflects Hungarian folk rhythm — the distinctive short-long pattern creates a characteristic uneven groove.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: String techniques expand traditional sound: pizzicato (plucked), col legno (wood of bow), sul ponticello (near bridge for glassy tone).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe how kodály and bartók are used in a piece of music you have studied. Use musical vocabulary. | Compare how two different pieces use kodály and bartók. Explain the effect in each case. | How could you use kodály and bartók in your own composition or performance? Explain your choices.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: A detailed description using precise musical vocabulary (e.g. specific terms from the AQA elements list), referencing a named piece with accurate observations about how the elements are used and their | A comparison of two pieces identifying similarities and differences in how kodály and bartók are used, explaining the different effects created in each musical context, using comparative language. | A practical application showing understanding of how kodály and bartók can be manipulated in composition or performance, with specific examples of choices made and their intended effect.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always use PRECISE musical vocabulary — not vague descriptions like it sounds nice Reference SPECIFIC musical elements when analysing any piece For listening questions: identify elements FIRST, then explain their effect For study pieces: know the context, structure and key features in detail For performing: focus on accuracy, expression and interpretation For composing: show development of ideas, not just repetition
